title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
source: Pañcatantra, Book 4 — retold for this book
text: On the bank of a wide river stood a rose-apple tree, and in it lived a cheerful monkey named Raktamukha. Every day a crocodile swam up to rest in the shade, and every day the monkey tossed him the sweetest, juiciest fruit. Soon they were the best of friends, talking until the sun went down.

The crocodile carried fruit home to his wife. ‘If the fruit is this sweet,’ she said, ‘how sweet must be the heart of the monkey who eats it every day! Bring me his heart.’ The crocodile was troubled, but he swam back and said, ‘Friend, my wife wishes to thank you. Climb on my back and come to dinner.’

Halfway across the deep water, the crocodile confessed the truth. The monkey’s heart thumped — but he kept his mind calm. ‘Oh dear friend,’ he said, ‘why didn’t you tell me? I keep my heart safe in the hollow of my tree! Take me back and I’ll fetch it.’

The crocodile turned around. The moment they reached the bank, the monkey leapt high into his tree. ‘A heart is not something you leave in a tree,’ he called down kindly, ‘and a friendship is not something you trade away.’
And so, little one, remember: a calm mind finds a way, even in deep water.

title: The Hare in the Moon
source: Śaśa Jātaka (Jātaka no. 316) — retold for this book
text: Long ago, in a forest by the mountains, four friends lived together: a monkey, a jackal, an otter and a gentle hare. The wise hare often said, ‘Let us share what we have with anyone who is hungry.’

One full-moon evening, a tired old traveller came to rest beneath their tree. The otter brought him fish from the river. The jackal brought a pot of curd he had found. The monkey brought ripe mangoes from the treetops.

But the little hare ate only grass, and grass is no food for a traveller. ‘I have nothing to give,’ he thought, ‘except myself.’ So he gathered sticks, lit a small fire, and said, ‘Friend, please accept me as your meal.’ And he leapt towards the flames.

But the fire did not burn him — it felt as cool as snow. The traveller stood up and shone with light. He was Sakka, king of the gods, who had come to see who had the kindest heart. ‘Your generosity should be remembered forever,’ he said.
Then he drew the shape of the hare upon the face of the moon. Tonight, little one, when we look at the full moon, we will see the hare there still — a picture of a heart that gives.

title: Rāma and the Squirrel
source: Folk tradition (South India); not found in Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa — retold for this book
text: When Rāma’s army built a bridge of stones across the ocean to Laṅkā, everyone helped. Mighty monkeys and bears lifted great boulders, and the sea rang with their work.
At the water’s edge, a tiny squirrel was busy too. She rolled in the wet sand, ran onto the bridge, and shook the sand off between the stones. Back and forth, back and forth, all day long.
A big monkey laughed. ‘Little one, what use is a few grains of sand when we carry mountains?’

Rāma saw it all. He lifted the squirrel gently in his palm. ‘Every grain fills a gap that no boulder can,’ he said. ‘Her love is as great as yours.’ He stroked her back with three fingers — and, the story says, that is why squirrels have three soft stripes to this day.
Little one, whatever you give with love — even something small — is never too little.

title: Hanumān’s Leap
source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Kiṣkindhā & Sundara Kāṇḍa — retold for this book
text: Sītā had been carried far across the ocean, and Rāma’s friends stood on the shore, wondering who could cross the endless water. Each said, ‘I can leap so far — but not that far.’

Hanumān sat quietly. He did not think he could do it either. Then the wise old bear Jāmbavān came and sat beside him. ‘Hanumān,’ he said, ‘you have forgotten who you are. Your strength was always inside you. Remember it.’
Hanumān closed his eyes and breathed slowly. He remembered — and as he remembered, he grew taller and stronger, until he stood like a mountain on the shore.
With Rāma’s name in his heart, he pressed his feet into the hill and leapt — over the waves, through the clouds, across the whole ocean — and landed safely on the other side.
Little one, there will be days when something feels too big. On those days, breathe slowly and remember: the strength you need is already inside you. (And your mother is learning this too.)
